title: Ad Nationes Libri Duo
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa002.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: | ubi tunc Christiani, cum res Romana tot historias laborum suorum subministrauit? ubi tunc Christiani, cum Hiera, Anaphe et Delos et Rhodos et Cea insulae multis cum milibus hominum pessum ierunt, uel quam Plato memorat maiorem Asia aut Africa in Atlantico mari mersam? cum Vulsinios de caelo, Pompeios de suo monte perfudit ignis? cum terrae motu mare Corinthium ereptum est? cum totum orbem cataclysmus aboleuit? ubi tunc, non dicam contemptores deorum Christiani, sed ipsi dei uestri, quos clade illa posteriores loca, oppida approbant in quibus nati morati sepulti sunt, etiam quae ccondiderunt?
passages.english: Where were the Christians then, when the Roman state supplied so many histories of its own troubles? Where were the Christians then, when the islands Hiera, Anaphe and Delos and Rhodes and Cea went to destruction with many thousands of people, or the [island] which Plato records, larger than Asia or Africa, sunk in the Atlantic sea? When fire from heaven poured over Volsinii, [and] over Pompeii from its own mountain? When the Corinthian sea was snatched away by an earthquake? When the deluge wiped out the whole world? Where then, I will not say were the Christians, despisers of the gods, but your gods themselves, who are proved later than that disaster by the places [and] towns in which they were born, lived, were buried, and even those which they founded?
passages.notes: The final sentence is difficult; the sense seems to be that the towns associated with the gods' births, lives and burials postdate the flood. 'ccondiderunt' is read as 'condiderunt'.

passages.original: Xenocrates Academicus bifariam facit, Olympios et Titanios,. qui de Caelo et Terra. Aegyptiorum plerique quattuor deos credunt, Solem et Lunam, Caelum ac Terram. cum reliquo igni superno deos ortos Democritus suspicatur, cuius instar uult esse naturam Zenon. unde et Varro ignem mundi animum facit, ut perinde in mundo ignis omnia gubernet sicut animus in nobis. atqui uanissime. namcum est, inquit, in nobis, ipsi sumus; cum exiuit, emorimur.
passages.english: Xenocrates the Academic makes [them] twofold, Olympians and Titans, who [are] from Heaven and Earth. Most of the Egyptians believe in four gods: the Sun and the Moon, Heaven and Earth. Democritus supposes that the gods arose together with the rest of the fire above, and Zeno wants nature to be like this [fire]. Hence Varro too makes fire the soul of the world, so that fire governs all things in the world just as the soul does in us. But this is utterly foolish. For when it is in us, he says, we ourselves exist; when it has gone out, we die.
passages.notes: The stray comma after 'Titanios' has been ignored. 'namcum' is read as 'nam cum'. The Latin 'inquit' ('he says') presumably refers to Varro, though the argument that follows is Tertullian's own.

passages.original: Quin ergo ad humaniorem aliquanto conuertimur | opinionem, quae de communi omnium sensu et simplici coniectura deducta uideatur? nam et Varro meminit eius, credi- | tam praeterea dicens elementorum diuinitatem, quod nihil omnino sine suffragio illorum gigni ali prouehi possit ad uitae humanae et terrae sationem, quando ne ipsa quidem corpora aut animas sufficere licuisset sine elementorum temperamento, quo habitatio ista mundi II circulorum condicionibus foederata praestatur, nisi quod hominum incolatui denegauit enormitas frigoris aut caoris, proptereaque deos credi solem, qui dies de suo cumulet, fruges caloribus expediat et annum stationibus seruet: lunam, solacium noctium, patrocinium Lmen]lsum gubernaculis: item sidera, signacula quaedam temporum ad ru notandorum: ipsum denique caelum, sub quo omnia, terram, super quam omnia, et quicquid illorum inter se ad commoda humana conspirat.
passages.english: Why then do we not turn to a somewhat more humane opinion, one which might seem to be drawn from the common sense of all and from simple conjecture? For Varro too mentions it, saying that the divinity of the elements was believed besides, because nothing at all could be begotten, nourished or brought forward for the sowing of human life and of the earth without their support, since not even bodies themselves or souls could have been sustained without the tempering of the elements, by which this habitation of the world, bound together by the conditions of its zones, is furnished, except that the excess of cold or heat has denied [some parts] to human settlement; and that for this reason the sun is believed [to be] a god, since it heaps up the days from its own [light], ripens the crops with its heat, and keeps the year by its stations; the moon, the comfort of the nights, the patron of [the months]; likewise the stars, certain marks of the seasons for noting [the times of] farming; and finally the sky itself, under which all things are, the earth, upon which all things are, and whatever of these works together for human benefit.
passages.notes: 'caoris' read as 'caloris'. 'patrocinium Lmen]lsum gubernaculis' is corrupt; taken as 'patrocinium mensum' (patron of the months), with 'gubernaculis' (helms/governance) left unclear. 'ad ru notandorum' read as 'ad rura notandorum' or similar (times for farming). 'mundi II circulorum': 'II' taken as a page or line mark.

passages.original: nam quae idonea auctoritas praecucurrit eiusmodi theologiae quam etiam fama destituit? quanti sunt qui norint uisu uel auditu Atarga Syrorum, Caelestem Afrorum, Varsutinam Maurorum, Obodan et Dus Arabum, Belenum Noricum, uel quos Varro ponit: Casiniensium Del, Narniensium Visidianum, Atinensium Numiternum, Asculanorum AnChariam, † et quam praeuerint, Vulsiniensium Nortiam, quorum ne nominum quidem dignitas humanis cognominibus distat?
passages.english: For what fit authority has gone before for a theology of this kind, which even report has abandoned? How many are there who know, by sight or by hearing, Atargatis of the Syrians, Caelestis of the Africans, Varsutina of the Moors, Obodas and Dusares of the Arabs, Belenus of Noricum, or those whom Varro lists: Delventinus of the Casinians, Visidianus of the Narnians, Numiternus of the Atinians, Ancharia of the Asculans, † and whom they have preferred(?), Nortia of the Volsinians, whose names do not even differ in dignity from human surnames?
passages.notes: 'Atarga', 'Del', 'Dus' appear truncated; read as Atargatis, Delventinus, Dusares. 'Varsutina' is otherwise unknown to me. The phrase marked † ('et quam praeuerint') is corrupt; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Sed enim manifestis uis sua adsistit. quos a primordio possunt non asserere nisi homines fuisse, recipiunt in diuinitatem, affirmando illos post mortem deos factos, ut Varro et qui cum eo somniauerunt. hic igitur consisto: si sunt allecti dei uestri in hoc nomen et numen, ut in ordinem senatorium,sapientia uestra esse concedatis iam necesse est aliquem summum dominatorem habentem allegendi potestatem et quasi Caesarem;
passages.english: But indeed, its own force stands by what is manifest. Those whom they cannot claim to have been anything but men from the beginning they receive into divinity, asserting that they were made gods after death, as Varro and those who dreamed along with him [do]. Here then I take my stand: if your gods were co-opted into this name and divine power, as into the senatorial order, you must now, by your own wisdom, concede that there is some supreme ruler holding the power of co-opting, a kind of Caesar;

passages.original: hunc uos de pyra in caelum subleuastis, | illa facilitate qua et alium ignis ex diuini ui confectum, qui pauca ee | ingenia commentus dicebatur mortuos ad uitam recurasse. is Apollinis filius, tam homo quam Iouis nepos, Saturni pronepos (uel potius, spurius ut incerto patre, ut Argiuus Socrates detulit, quippe expositum repertum, turpius Ioue educatum, canino scilicet ubere), merito, id quod nemo negare potest, fulmine haustus est. malus Iuppiter Optimus hic rursus est, impius in nepotem, inuidus in artificem.
passages.english: Him you raised from the pyre into heaven, with the same ease with which [you raised] another, consumed by fire from divine power, who was said to have devised a few clever arts and brought the dead back to life. This son of Apollo, as much a man as [he was] grandson of Jupiter and great-grandson of Saturn (or rather a bastard, since his father was uncertain, as Socrates of Argos reported, being in fact found exposed and, more shamefully than Jupiter, reared at a dog's teat), was deservedly, as no one can deny, swallowed up by the thunderbolt. Here again Jupiter Best is wicked: impious toward his grandson, envious toward a craftsman.
passages.notes: 'ee' read as a stray mark. 'ex diuini ui' read as 'ex diuina ui'. The second figure is Asclepius; 'hunc' refers to Heracles from the preceding context.
